Josephus interpolation: the majority view (partial authenticity: a neutral core of 18.3.3 with Christian additions such as 'if it be lawful to call him a man', 'He was [the] Christ', 'he appeared to them alive again the third day') and the near-consensus authenticity of 20.9.1 are standard (see e.g. J. P. Meier, A Marginal Jew vol. 1, 1991, ch. 3; the 10th-century Arabic version of Agapius, published by Shlomo Pines, 1971). A minority, e.g. Richard Carrier, argue 'who was called Christ' in 20.9.1 is also an interpolation. Josephus's Antiquities dated AD 93–94 (Ant. 20.267: thirteenth year of Domitian). Reviewer: confirm wording 'most scholars' / 'widely accepted'.

Pliny text: Gutenberg #2811, 'Letters of Pliny', translator William Melmoth (died 1799; translation 1746), revised by F. C. T. Bosanquet (Bohn's Classical Library, 1878). I could not confirm Bosanquet's death date; the revision was published long before 1929. In this edition the letters are numbered X.XCVII and X.XCVIII; standard numbering is Letters 10.96 and 10.97. Two obvious transcription slips in the Gutenberg file were corrected: "officiate'" -> "officiate" and "Secundtis" -> "Secundus" (Trajan's reply). Reviewer may prefer to restore the file text exactly. Pliny claims: governor of Bithynia-Pontus about AD 110–113; letter usually dated about AD 112; 'two female slaves ... said to officiate' translates Latin 'ministrae' (often rendered deaconesses). 'A form of prayer to Christ, as to a divinity' renders 'carmen Christo quasi deo', often translated 'a hymn to Christ as to a god'. Pliny's dates (about 61 – about 113) are approximate. 'About eighty years after the cross' assumes crucifixion about AD 30 and letter about 112.

Mark is the earliest Gospel: majority scholarly view (Markan priority), stated as 'most scholars think'. Gospel dating 'roughly forty to seventy years after Jesus' assumes Mark about AD 70 and John about 90–100; some scholars date Mark earlier.

1 Corinthians written about AD 53–55 (from Ephesus, 1 Cor 16:8). The early dating of the formula in 15:3–8 (often to within a few years of the crucifixion) is widely held, including by sceptical scholars; e.g. Gerd Lüdemann and Bart Ehrman (How Jesus Became God, 2014) treat it as pre-Pauline tradition. 'Largely forgotten' is the standard account; some movements were known.

Messiah: composed 22 August to 14 September 1741 ('about three weeks'); libretto by Charles Jennens from the King James Bible and the Prayer Book psalter; first performance Dublin, 13 April 1742, in aid of prisoners' debt relief, Mercer's Hospital and the Charitable Infirmary. Closing choruses 'Worthy is the Lamb' and 'Blessing and honour' set Revelation 5:12–13, ending with the 'Amen' fugue. Messiah opens with Isaiah 40:1–5 ('Comfort ye'). Sources: Donald Burrows, Handel: Messiah (Cambridge, 1991).

Mozart Requiem: commissioned anonymously in 1791 through an intermediary by Count Franz von Walsegg, who is thought to have intended to present it as his own in memory of his wife; Mozart died 5 December 1791; he left the Lacrimosa after 8 bars; completed by Franz Xaver Süssmayr. Sources: Christoph Wolff, Mozart's Requiem (1994). 'Seems to have meant' is deliberately cautious.
